chapter.title: Putting It Together
chapter.description: A short review of the pieces and how they combine into an interactive component.

blocks.text: Events and conditionals are the two halves of interactivity: an event changes state, and the conditional decides what the new state looks like on screen.

blocks.caption: Two pieces of state, two conditionals, two handlers.

blocks.text: Notice what is not in state
`isTooShort` is derived during render rather than stored. There is no way for it to fall out of sync with `value`, and no handler has to remember to update it.

items: Event props take a function and receive a synthetic event.
`preventDefault` stops the browser default; `stopPropagation` stops the bubble.
Use a ternary for either/or, `&&` for show-or-nothing, and early returns for loading and error paths.
A changing `key` remounts a subtree, which is the tidiest way to reset it.

blocks.text: Conditional classes are just string expressions. For anything beyond one or two toggles, a helper such as `classnames` keeps it readable.

blocks.code:
<button className={isActive ? "tab tab-active" : "tab"}>Overview</button>

// With a helper
<button className={classNames("tab", { "tab-active": isActive })}>
  Overview
</button>

blocks.text: React matches elements between renders by position and type. If the type at a position is the same, React reuses the existing DOM node and its state. If it differs, it destroys the old one and builds a new one.
Sometimes resetting is exactly what you want - for example, clearing a form when the selected record changes. Give the element a `key` that changes, and React rebuilds it with fresh state.

blocks.code:
// Each time userId changes, the form remounts with empty state
<ProfileForm key={userId} userId={userId} />

blocks.text: A changing `key` is the cleanest way to reset a subtree. It beats an effect that manually clears half a dozen state values.
